Thank you for your careful and insightful reviews. We sincerely appreciate **your recognition of our paper's key contributions**, particularly the clear definition of Preference Rigidity. We are also deeply encouraged by your view that **our paper demonstrates a clever engineering contribution**. We sincerely hope that our response addresses your concerns.

> W1: Given that the training data (Table 7) includes large datasets like RLAIF-V, was any data contamination check performed to ensure that (near) duplicates from VL-RewardBench or Multimodal RewardBench were not present in the training set?

Thank you for raising this insightful point. Following your suggestion, we re-examined the VL-RewardBench dataset and found that its hallucination subset was partially constructed using RLAIF-V. In our training pipeline, we had sampled 40,000 examples from RLAIF-V. By applying a data contamination check using a 3-gram Jaccard threshold of 0.8, we identified 121 overlapping samples between our training data and VL-RewardBench. In contrast, we found no data leakage issues with Multimodal RewardBench.

To address this, we removed all overlapping samples and retrained the model. **We observed a small performance drop on the hallucination subset of VL-RewardBench (from 94.2% to 91.1%), while performance on the other VL-RewardBench subsets and on Multimodal RewardBench remained unaffected. The model therefore retains strong overall performance, which further demonstrates the robustness and generalization ability of our constructed Omni-RewardData.** We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We will update our training data to remove all potential leakage cases in the revised version.

> W2: The authors' own Omni-RewardData (Table 7) appears to only contain data for T2T, TI2T, T2I, and T2V tasks. The key modalities used to demonstrate this gap in the benchmark (T2A, T23D, TI2I) are absent from the training data.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful observation. The main reason that T2A, T23D, and TI2I preference data are not included in Omni-RewardData is that such multimodal preference annotations are extremely scarce and difficult to collect at scale in practice. **Consequently, our dataset construction focuses on modalities for which high-quality preference data can be reliably obtained.** Moreover, we explicitly included these scarce modalities in Omni-RewardBench through human annotations.

Despite this limitation, one of the central findings of our study is that reward models trained solely on the more accessible modalities, including T2T, TI2T, T2I, and T2V, exhibit strong generalization to the scarce modalities that are absent from the training set. **Our results demonstrate the feasibility of achieving cross-task generalization even without explicit supervision from these modalities.**

Thank you for your careful and insightful reviews. We appreciate your recognition that our work, including the benchmark, dataset, and trained reward models, **will be valuable for the alignment community**. **Your assessment that the paper is nearly of spotlight/oral quality is truly encouraging and motivates us to further refine our work**. We sincerely hope that our response addresses your concerns.

> W1: There are several recent works that move beyond binary preference pairs and homogenous modeling, though they do not use fully free-form preferences. How does Omni Reward modeling fit in this landscape, as pluralistic alignment to diverse human values is becoming more and more relevant? I suggest adding a comment in the conclusion or brief discussion in the revision about this.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. Positioning our work within the broader landscape of heterogeneous preference modeling and pluralistic alignment is indeed meaningful and can further clarify the contribution of Omni-Reward.

As AI systems continue to advance in capability and societal impact, ensuring that they can faithfully align with the diverse values, goals, and perspectives of different users has become increasingly critical. This shift places new demands on reward models, requiring them to move beyond traditional binary preference learning and instead capture heterogeneous, multi-dimensional human preferences across varying contexts and scenarios. PAL proposes a pluralistic alignment framework that leverages an ideal-point formulation together with mixture modeling over shared preference prototypes, allowing reward models to represent heterogeneous human preferences and generalize to new users with only a few comparisons. SyncPL introduces a criteria-based preference tree for reward modeling, where each path corresponds to a synthesized-criteria reasoning trajectory.

**In line with this emerging direction, Omni-Reward extends heterogeneous preference alignment into the omni-modal setting by enabling reward modeling across text, image, video, audio, and 3D tasks using rich free-form natural-language preference descriptions rather than binary comparisons. Our benchmark further provides a unified and comprehensive evaluation suite for assessing pluralistic alignment across diverse modalities, and our trained reward models offer practical tools for advancing research in heterogeneous preference learning.** We appreciate the reviewer’s guidance and have added a dedicated subsection on Heterogeneous Preference Alignment to the Related Work section to more clearly highlight this connection.

> Q1: Is there a specific reason you did not use Pick-a-Pic (v1 or v2) for the text-to-image preference data or ImageReward as a reward model baseline (Tab 1).

Pick-a-Pic is an important and widely used T2I preference dataset. The main reason we did not include it in our construction is that Pick-a-Pic is currently not available on HuggingFace. Additionally, HPDv2 has a similar data format and serves as an effective substitute while being readily accessible. Regarding ImageReward, we also evaluate it as a baseline on OmniRewardBench following your suggestion. Its performance on T2I is comparable to PickScore. We will include ImageReward as an additional baseline in the revised version of the paper.

| **Model**       | **T2I w/ Ties** | **T2I w/o Ties** |
| --------------- | --------------- | ---------------- |
| PickScore       | 60.12           | 69.61            |
| HPSv2           | 63.85           | 73.70            |
| **ImageReward** | 60.51           | 69.16            |

> Q2: I am curious how does Qwen 3 Omni perform in the T2A and TA2T tasks? I do not expect this experiment in the rebuttal, but it would be nice to include (at least for the audio-specific tasks).

This is an interesting and insightful suggestion. Following the reviewer’s comment, we conduct an evaluation of Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on the T2A and TA2T tasks under the w/ Tie setting. The results indicate that the model performs very well on both tasks, demonstrating its potential to serve as a strong base model for an omni-modal reward model.

| **Model**                       | **TA2T** | **T2A** |
| ------------------------------- | -------- | ------- |
| **Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct** | 63.31    | 46.35   |
| Qwen2.5-Omni-7B                 | 59.66    | 32.60   |
| GPT-4o                          | 62.75    | 44.53   |
| Omni-RewardModel-BT             | 70.59    | 63.99   |

summary.value: The paper reframes reward modeling as criterion-conditioned, omni-modal preference learning to overcome modality imbalance and rigid, binary notions of “helpfulness.” It contributes three components. (1) Omni-RewardBench: a five-modality, nine-task benchmark in which each pairwise comparison is explicitly conditioned on a free-form textual criterion. (2) Omni-RewardData: 317K preference pairs combining general supervision with instruction-tuning data that teaches models to read and follow criteria. (3) Omni-RewardModel: a discriminative Bradley-Terry scorer and a generative, critic-style RM trained with RL that verbalizes brief reasoning before deciding.

strengths.value: The benchmark is notably broad (five modalities and nine tasks) with human-labeled pairs and explicit free-form criteria, evaluated under both w/ ties and w/o ties settings, which is a clear advance over prior suites. The dataset combines large general preference pools with an instruction-tuning subset whose criteria/labels are multi-model verified, improving criterion-following. Empirically, the study is broad, and the BT variant achieves strong accuracy on the new bench and competitive results on public suites.

weaknesses.value: Human annotations come from a small PhD group; after quality control, disagreements are removed, yielding consensus-only labels that may under-sample ambiguous cases. Some modality imbalance remains in distribution. The instruction-tuning split relies on GPT-4o-generated criteria/labels which could encode stylistic biases (though mitigated via verification). Finally, beyond the CoT ablation, the paper would benefit from richer qualitative error analyses across modalities to illuminate failure modes.

summary.value: This paper aims to solve two core challenges in aligning Artificial Intelligence (AI) behaviors with Reward Models (RMs): (1) Modality Imbalance , where existing RMs focus primarily on text and image, with limited support for modalities like video and audio; and (2) Preference Rigidity, where models trained on fixed binary preference pairs fail to capture complex and personalized preferences.

strengths.value:
1. One of the paper's most valuable contributions is its clear definition of "Preference Rigidity". Existing RMs typically learn a static reward function $r(x, y)$. This paper proposes transforming it into a dynamic, controllable function $r(x, y | c)$, where $c$ is a free-form text criterion. 

2.Omni-RewardBench is a direct and successful implementation of the problem defined above. It is the first benchmark to systematically evaluate RMs

3. The 69K instruction-tuning dataset built to address "preference rigidity" is a clever engineering contribution

weaknesses.value:
1.The model achieves SOTA on VL-RewardBench. Given that the training data (Table 7) includes large datasets like RLAIF-V, was any data contamination check performed to ensure that (near) duplicates from VL-RewardBench or Multimodal RewardBench were not present in the training set?

2.The authors' own Omni-RewardData (Table 7) appears to only contain data for T2T, TI2T, T2I, and T2V tasks. The key modalities used to demonstrate this gap in the benchmark (T2A, T23D, TI2I) are absent from the training data.

summary.value:
This paper addresses two challenges: (1) modality imbalance and (2) preference rigidity by introducing `Omni-RewardData` and `Omni-RewardBench`. To tackle modality imbalance, the authors collect a large-scale multimodal preference dataset and benchmark across 9 tasks. To address preference rigidity, the authors collect human preference pairs with free-form preference descriptions to enable more fine-grained analysis of human preferences.

The authors systematically evaluate the performance limitations of current reward models (RMs) on multi-modal scenarios and find that they perform poorly on Omni-RewardBench. More importantly, performance varies significantly across different modalities—a phenomenon they conceptualize as "modality imbalance".

strengths.value:
1. Introduces free-form preference descriptions to resolve the preference rigidity issue and enable RMs to learn more fine-grained human preferences.
---
2. Collects a human preference dataset from diverse tasks (including T2T, TI2T, T2I, T2V), allowing the model to generalize to novel multi-modal scenarios and adapt to human preferences across different tasks.
---
3. Introduces synthetic instruction-tuning data to allow RMs to adapt to customized evaluation and fine-grained user preferences.
---
4. Provides clear ablation analysis on incorporating both mixed multimodal data and synthetic instruction-tuning user specifications.

weaknesses.value:
1. The 3.7K samples in `Omni-RewardBench` were collected from only three PhD students in computer science, which may not reflect general human preferences. The diversity of the benchmark is questionable.
---
2. The mixture of the multimodal preference dataset is lacking an explanation. What would be a good multimodal data mixture ratio?
---
3. Table 3 provides concise evidence for the authors' claim that "using mixed multimodal data leads to significantly better generalization across tasks." However, more rigorous analysis is needed to determine how each modality's task data contributes to preference prediction in other modalities.

summary.value:
This paper proposes Omni-Reward, a generalist omni-modal reward modeling framework that introduces a new benchmark with free-form preferences, a large multimodal preference dataset, and both discriminative and generative reward models. These components enable stronger and more flexible reward modeling across text, image, video, audio, and 3D modalities.

The paper received unanimous positive evaluation from all the reviewers, even before rebuttal. Most reviewers’ concerns focus on missing details and requests for clarification, all of which have been addressed in the rebuttal.

Thank you for the careful follow-up experiments and the detailed clarifications. I appreciate the effort in re-running the contamination checks and reporting the new results. Despite the unavoidable limitations in annotation resources (which I fully understand is a common practical constraint), I do find the overall framework quite insightful. In particular, the paper’s articulation of Preference Rigidity is conceptually clear and, in my view, one of the most compelling aspects of the work. It provides a useful lens for thinking about how current RMs implicitly encode fixed preference structures, and I believe this perspective will be valuable for the community.

Given the strength of the idea and the clarity added through the rebuttal, I am willing to raise my score to 8, consistent with reviewer 2fvx. I look forward to seeing this work potentially appear as a spotlight/highlight at the conference : ).

> Q1: Omni-RewardBench covers more modalities/tasks than prior human-labeled suites but with a comparable or even smaller total size. Are per-task and per-modality sample sizes sufficient?

We would like to emphasize that Omni-RewardBench is fully human-annotated, with all preference pairs curated under carefully defined criteria and consistent annotation guidelines. The annotation process was rigorous and time-consuming, requiring substantial manual effort from our team to ensure the quality, consistency, and reliability of the data. Unlike automatically generated preference data, our benchmark captures rich, fine-grained human preferences across multiple dimensions. Importantly, **our experimental results exhibit clear and meaningful performance differences across tasks and modalities, demonstrating that the per-task and per-modality sample sizes are sufficient to expose distinct model behaviors and reliably evaluate reward model performance.**

> Q2: What were the exact quality-control rules for filtering criteria and preference labels? And how does that affect the benchmark data quality?

As illustrated in Figure 3, our annotation pipeline consists of two key stages: Criteria Annotation and Preference Annotation. Across these stages, we removed a substantial portion of the samples to ensure high data quality.

1.  In the **Criteria Annotation** stage, we filtered out samples whose annotated criteria were judged to be either too vague or overly specific, as such criteria would reduce the consistency and usefulness of the resulting preference data.

2.  In the **Preference Annotation** stage, we further discarded samples on which annotators could not reach agreement, i.e., cases where the final preference labels were inconsistent or ambiguous across annotators. This guarantees that all retained labels reflect strong consensus.

> Q3: What is the proportion of ties within the preference labels per task/modality?

Thank you for raising this point. We apologize for not including this detail earlier and now provide the full tie proportion breakdown in the table below.

| Task    | # Total | # w/ Ties | # w/o Ties |
| ------- | ------- | --------- | ---------- |
| T2T     | 417     | 51        | 366        |
| TI2T    | 528     | 98        | 430        |
| TV2T    | 443     | 63        | 380        |
| TA2T    | 357     | 23        | 334        |
| T2I     | 509     | 68        | 441        |
| T2V     | 529     | 63        | 466        |
| T2A     | 411     | 15        | 396        |
| T23D    | 302     | 38        | 264        |
| TI2I    | 229     | 22        | 207        |
| Overall | 3725    | 441       | 3284       |

Thank you for your careful and insightful reviews. We sincerely appreciate **your recognition of our paper’s key contributions**, including the introduction of free-form preference descriptions to address preference rigidity. We are also deeply encouraged by **your appreciation of our ablation analysis on mixed multimodal data**. We sincerely hope that our response addresses your concerns.

> W1: The 3.7K samples in Omni-RewardBench were collected from only three PhD students in computer science, which may not reflect general human preferences. The diversity of the benchmark is questionable.

Thank you for pointing this out. We acknowledge that the current annotations were produced by a relatively small group of PhD students. The annotation of the entire dataset was a time-intensive process that required substantial manual effort from our team. Given the constraints of limited resources, we took extensive measures to ensure the quality and consistency of the annotations. Detailed annotation guidelines and examples are provided in Appendix D.2 to ensure that all participants fully understood the process, thereby ensuring both the diversity and high quality of the annotations. Annotators are explicitly instructed to generate diverse and fine-grained criteria wherever possible, which further contributed to the richness of the preference data. **As shown in Figure 1, the data distribution visualization demonstrates the broad coverage and diversity of the samples included in OmniRewardBench.**

> W2: The mixture of the multimodal preference dataset is lacking an explanation. What would be a good multimodal data mixture ratio?

Thank you for raising this important point. Our multimodal data mixture ratio is designed according to three principles:

1.  **Alignment with real-world task distribution.** We upweight the TI2T data because image understanding is a dominant and representative multimodal task, and TI2T responses contain rich, fine-grained textual feedback grounded in visual content, providing highly informative supervision for learning reward models.

2.  **Data availability.** We maintain a substantial proportion of T2T and T2I data, as these modalities are widely available and well-established in existing preference datasets, which helps maintain strong general preference modeling capabilities.

3.  **Maintaining modality balance.** We additionally include a small amount of T2V data, not to improve video-specific performance, but to enhance the model’s robustness to multi-image inputs.

**Overall, our curation experience suggests that large, high-quality data are crucial for establishing strong core preference modeling capabilities, while adding smaller amounts of scarce modalities further enhances the model’s performance on those specific input types.**

> W3: More rigorous analysis is needed to determine how each modality's task data contributes to preference prediction in other modalities.

Thank you for the helpful suggestion. Based on the ablation results in Table 3 and Table 10, we conduct a more detailed analysis to better understand how each modality contributes to cross-modal reward modeling. We find that T2T and TI2T are particularly helpful for **multimodal understanding** tasks such as **TV2T** and **TA2T**, indicating strong transfer to other understanding tasks. In contrast, T2I and T2V mainly enhance **multimodal generation** evaluation, especially on tasks like **T2A** and **T23D**, demonstrating their effectiveness in generalizing to generation tasks. Moreover, combining these modalities provides complementary supervision signals that jointly strengthen **cross-modal generalization**. We also observe that even a small amount of synthetic instruction-tuning data plays a critical role in further enhancing the model’s ability to score responses according to fine-grained evaluation criteria. We will incorporate this analysis into the revised version to more clearly highlight the cross-modal contributions of each data modality.

Thank you for your careful and insightful reviews. We are deeply encouraged by your recognition that **our work represents a clear advance over prior suites**, due to the supported modalities and the explicit free-form criteria it incorporates. We sincerely hope that our response addresses your concerns.

> W1: Human annotations come from a small PhD group.

Thank you for pointing this out. We acknowledge that the current annotations were produced by a relatively small group of PhD students. The annotation of the entire dataset was a time-intensive process that required substantial manual effort from our team. Given the constraints of limited resources, we took extensive measures to ensure the quality and consistency of the annotations. Detailed annotation guidelines and examples are provided in Appendix D.2 to ensure that all participants fully understood the process, thereby ensuring both the diversity and high quality of the annotations.

> W2: After quality control, disagreements are removed, yielding consensus-only labels that may under-sample ambiguous cases.

We removed disagreements during quality control to ensure high consistency in preference annotations, as our primary goal was to improve the overall quality of the preference data. We fully agree with the reviewer’s perspective, and acknowledge that preference ambiguity is a common phenomenon in real-world human feedback. Therefore, we plan to incorporate ambiguous or partially conflicting preference cases into the future version of the training data, which may enable reward models to become more robust when handling diverse or inconsistent human preferences.

> W3: Some modality imbalance remains in distribution.

Thank you for pointing this out. Due to the inherent difficulty of collecting high-quality data across multiple modalities, some imbalance in the distribution of preference pairs is unavoidable. While some imbalance remains, **our dataset maintains a relatively balanced distribution across modalities, especially when compared to the significant disparities commonly observed in real-world data availability between modalities such as images and audio**. Moreover, in our evaluation, we report per-task performance to ensure that models are assessed fairly within each modality, thereby reducing the impact of sample size differences on overall performance comparisons.

> W4: The instruction-tuning split relies on GPT-4o-generated criteria/labels which could encode stylistic biases (though mitigated via verification).

We agree with your concern. To construct a large-scale training set, we employed GPT-4o to generate free-form instructions $c$ that reflect user preferences supporting either $y_1$ or $y_2$, along with the corresponding label $p$. To mitigate potential stylistic biases introduced by relying solely on GPT-4o, we incorporated a multi-model verification process. Specifically, we used GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Gemma-3-12B-it to verify the consistency of each tuple $(c, x, y_1, y_2)$ with its label $p$, thereby reducing potential errors and biases in the instruction generation process. We plan to further explore the use of multiple models for constructing preference data to better avoid the stylistic bias issue.

> W5: Finally, beyond the CoT ablation, the paper would benefit from richer qualitative error analyses across modalities to illuminate failure modes.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We agree that a richer qualitative analysis is crucial for illuminating the failure modes of current models. Following this recommendation, we conduct a detailed error analysis on our Omni-RewardBench and have identified several recurring patterns of failure. Below, we summarize two prominent failure modes with illustrative examples.

1.  **Positional Bias**: We observed that some models exhibit a strong positional bias, systematically favoring the response presented first, irrespective of its actual quality. For example, when evaluating two candidate audio responses, open-source models frequently assign a higher score to Response 1 even when Response 2 more accurately fulfills the user's instruction.

2.  **Over-reliance on Holistic Visual Quality**: In vision-centric tasks, we found that models often prioritize overall perceptual aesthetics over adherence to specific, fine-grained criteria outlined in the prompt. For instance, when asked to evaluate two images based on a precise editing instruction, a model may incorrectly favor a higher-resolution image that fails to implement the instruction, over a lower-resolution counterpart that correctly executes the requested change. This indicates a tendency to confound general image quality with task-specific alignment.

summary.value: This work proposes Omni-Reward, an omni-modal reward model benchmark that extends beyond image and text modalities and supports free-form preferences instead of status quo binary preferences as well as a new dataset Omni-RewardData containing preference and instruction tuning multimodal data pairs. The authors use this data to train Omni-RewardModel, which has both discriminative and generative reward model variants, that shows strong empirical performance on their own proposed benchmark, as well as public reward model benchmarks.

strengths.value:
* This work proposes an omni-reward model that covers 5 modalities. While multi-modal RMs are not new [1-2], no prior work to my knowledge also covers audio and 3D modality tasks, which is novel and a valuable contribution. The authors also contextualize their work with respect to these prior works (L309-312)
* The paper is well written and easy to follow
* The dataset contribution is valuable to train multi-modal reward models, which the authors demonstrate via the Omni-RewardModel. 
* The trained Omni-RewardModel shows strong performance on the proposed Omni-RewardBench (Tab 1), often beating open source models while lagging behind proprietary models on a few tasks, as well as VL-RewardBench (Tab 2) where it achieves state-of-the-art performance

title.value: Rebuttal Summary for the New Area Chair (Part 1)

comment.value:
Dear AC,

We sincerely regret the unexpected termination of the discussion period and greatly appreciate your dedication throughout the review process. Given the current situation, we fully understand that it may be helpful for you to quickly become familiar with the key points of our work and the progress of the rebuttal. **To better assist your evaluation, we have prepared a clear and concise summary of the entire discussion.** Our summary consists of three parts: **an overview of the discussion process, the strengths identified by the reviewers, and the common concerns they raised**.

### **An Overview of the Discussion Process**

**During the discussion, we were grateful to receive responses from Reviewer 2fvx and Reviewer fd9w. We are also very grateful that both reviewers expressed the view that our paper has the potential to be a spotlight/highlight paper.**

1. Reviewer 2fvx initially stated that the work had "**no significant weaknesses**" and emphasized the importance of contextualizing Omni-Reward within heterogeneous preference learning. After reading our rebuttal, Reviewer 2fvx was glad to see that Omni-Reward performs strongly in audio tasks and further acknowledged our efforts toward improving diversity and quality. **Reviewer 2fvx considered the work valuable to the community, regarded it as "a 9/10 in quality" with the potential to be a spotlight/highlight paper**, and suggested that more diverse preference collection could further strengthen it. **Reviewer 2fvx ultimately maintained an overall score of 8/10.**

2. Reviewer fd9w initially inquired about whether a data contamination check had been conducted and highlighted that **one of the most valuable contributions of the paper is its clear definition of "Preference Rigidity"**. After reading our rebuttal, Reviewer fd9w appreciated our effort in re-running the contamination checks and reporting the updated results. Reviewer fd9w found **the overall framework insightful** and noted that the articulation of Preference Rigidity provides a useful lens for understanding how current reward models implicitly encode fixed preference structures, **a perspective considered valuable for the community**. Given the strength of the idea and the additional clarity provided through the rebuttal, **Reviewer fd9w revised the original score from 6/10 (confidence 3) to 8/10 (confidence 4) and expressed the same interest in seeing the work potentially appear as a spotlight/highlight at the conference.**

Unfortunately, due to the unexpected termination of the discussion period, we did not have the opportunity to receive responses from Reviewer qACk and Reviewer gnxg.

### **Strengths Highlighted by the Reviewers**

Reviewers unanimously recognized the strength of our contributions across evaluation, data, and model design, as well as the novelty of our free-form preference framework and the strong empirical results. We are sincerely grateful that **half of the reviewers explicitly recognizing the work as being of spotlight/oral quality** (Reviewers 2fvx and fd9w). We truly appreciate that, in recognition of the clarity provided in our rebuttal, Reviewer fd9w raised the score from 6 to 8, resulting in the ratings of **8, 8, 6, and 6**.

1. **Novel Conceptual Contribution**: The paper’s clear definition of "Preference Rigidity" and the shift from static binary comparisons to criterion-conditioned, free-form preference descriptions are considered valuable and insightful contributions (Reviewers fd9w, qACk, gnxg). 

2. **Broad Benchmark Coverage**: The proposed Omni-RewardBench is recognized as a clear advance over prior suites, notably for its broad coverage of five modalities (including under-explored modalities like Audio and 3D) and nine tasks, all fully human-labeled (Reviewers gnxg, 2fvx, fd9w). 

3. **High-Quality Dataset Construction**: The construction of Omni-RewardData is highlighted as a valuable and clever engineering contribution. Reviewers specifically appreciate the combination of general preference pairs with synthetic instruction-tuning data, which enables models to adapt to fine-grained user specifications (Reviewers fd9w, 2fvx, qACk, gnxg). 

4. **Strong Empirical Performance and Generalization**: The trained Omni-RewardModel exhibits strong empirical performance, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks such as Omni-RewardBench and VL-RewardBench, and demonstrates effective generalization to novel multimodal scenarios (Reviewers 2fvx, gnxg, qACk). 

5. **Clarity and Quality of Presentation**: The paper is praised for being well-written and easy to follow (Reviewers 2fvx, qACk).
